raw_case_text: A 9-year-old boy presented with fever and malaise in September 2019. After 2 weeks, this was accompanied by a painful and tender left anterior cervical lymphadenopathy. He was diagnosed with bacterial lymphadenitis by a local physician and was prescribed ceftriaxone and methylprednisolone. Oral antipyretics did not provide relief. Ten days later, there was persistent low-grade fever (axillary temperature, >=37.5 C) with gradual lymph node enlargement. No apparent recent weight loss was observed. This prompted admission on the 18th day of illness at our hospital. Travel and exposure history was unremarkable. Physical examination was normal except for a slightly tender, 2.0 x 1.0 cm left anterior cervical lymph node. Laboratory test results showed a normal C-reactive protein (CRP), white blood cell (WBC) count of 3,060/mm3 with a low absolute neutrophil count of 1,010/mm3, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 21 mm/h. T-spot examination and purified protein derivative were negative. Serologic tests were negative for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), and hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. He underwent lymph node biopsy, which revealed a large classic necrotic focus and proliferation of surrounding tissue cells suggestive of KFD (Figure 1). Supportive therapy, including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and intravenous dexamethasone (10 mg), was administered. His symptoms gradually improved. He was subsequently discharged with naproxen and a tapering dose of prednisone. However, he was readmitted 10 days later due to fever recurrence. He was treated with intravenous pentahydrate cefazolin and continuous oral prednisone therapy. Improvement was noted until the 8th day of re-admission when he had a transient headache with nausea and vomiting. Neck stiffness and Kernig's sign were absent. Physical examinations and neurologic examinations did not reveal any other abnormalities. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed lymphocytic predominant pleocytosis (100 mm3, 77% lymphocytes), proteins of 86 mg/dL, and glucose of 43.24 mg/dL. Cerebrospinal fluid studies were negative for viral, bacterial, or fungal infections. CSF culture was sterile, and PCR for viral agents was negative. Neuroimaging revealed prominent meningeal enhancement. Additional medications, including naproxen, meropenem, acyclovir, and mannitol, were administered to decrease intracranial pressure. After 10 days, his condition improved significantly, and CSF analysis was normal. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was normal. The patient remained well on follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 9-year-old boy presented in September 2019 with an 18-day history of persistent fever, malaise, and painful left anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and subsequently developed recurrent fever, headache, nausea, and vomiting from aseptic meningitis on readmission.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Following 2 weeks of fever and malaise, the patient developed painful left anterior cervical lymphadenopathy that failed outpatient ceftriaxone, methylprednisolone, and antipyretics, leading to admission on day 18 of illness. Discharged improved on naproxen and a prednisone taper after biopsy diagnosis of Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease (KFD), he was readmitted 10 days later with recurrent fever and developed acute headache, nausea, and vomiting on day 8 of readmission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical, travel, and exposure history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial admission: 18 days of fever (>=37.5 °C), malaise, and tender left cervical swelling without weight loss. Readmission day 8: recurrent fever, transient headache, nausea, and vomiting.

objective.physical_examination: Initial admission: axillary temperature >=37.5 °C and a slightly tender 2.0 x 1.0 cm left anterior cervical lymph node; remainder of exam normal. Readmission day 8: normal neurological exam without neck stiffness or Kernig's sign.
objective.routine_investigations: Normal CRP, leukopenia with WBC 3,060/mm3 and low ANC 1,010/mm3, and ESR 21 mm/h. T-SPOT.TB, PPD skin test, and serologies for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), and hepatitis B virus (HBV) were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Cervical lymph node biopsy demonstrated a large classic paracortical necrotic focus with surrounding histiocytic proliferation diagnostic of Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease (KFD). During readmission day 8 headache/vomiting, lumbar puncture revealed lymphocytic-predominant CSF pleocytosis (100 cells/mm3, 77% lymphocytes), elevated CSF protein (86 mg/dL), CSF glucose 43.24 mg/dL, sterile bacterial/fungal cultures, and negative CSF viral PCRs (repeat CSF after 10 days of therapy was normal). Neuroimaging showed prominent leptomeningeal enhancement with normal brain parenchyma on follow-up brain MRI.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease (histiocytic necrotizing lymphadenitis, confirmed by cervical lymph node biopsy; TB, EBV, CMV, and HBV excluded) complicated upon readmission by KFD-associated aseptic meningitis (confirmed by CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis of 100/mm3, elevated protein 86 mg/dL, meningeal enhancement on neuroimaging, and negative CSF viral PCRs and bacterial/fungal cultures). Treated initially with NSAIDs (naproxen), IV dexamethasone (10 mg), and oral prednisone, and during the aseptic meningitis flare with naproxen, prednisone, mannitol, and empiric meropenem and acyclovir, achieving complete clinical and CSF normalization within 10 days and sustained recovery on follow-up.
